mainKeyword: best solar panel for travel trailer
guideTitle: Best Solar Panels for Travel Trailers (2026)
metaTitle: Best Solar Panels for Travel Trailers (2026)
metaDescription: Six solar panels and kits for travel trailers, from a 100W starter to two-panel 400W sets, compared on roof fit, heat loss and the long cable run to the tongue.
expertTake: The HQST 400W pair is the best travel trailer choice because two compact 200W N-type panels give a serious array in a small roof footprint. The ECO-WORTHY 200W kit is the value pick for a first install. Anyone who only camps with hookups should skip a roof array and fit a better battery charger.
introParagraphs: A travel trailer sits between a van and a big motorhome in roof size, and it has one quirk that shapes every solar decision: the batteries usually live up on the tongue, many feet from the roof. That long run between panel and battery makes wire gauge, voltage and controller placement matter more than they do in a van.

Trailers also tend to be parked for long stays in the sun, which stresses panels thermally. We evaluated each pick on its spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, comparing roof footprint, temperature behavior, kit contents, portable alternatives and how well each handles expansion toward a larger array.

products.name: HQST 400W Set, Two 200W N-Type Panels
products.description:
A pair of 200W panels, each only 46.3 by 30.1 inches, gives a trailer 400W without eating the roof. HQST uses N-type 16-busbar cells with up to 25.4% efficiency and Grade A+ quality, and the 1.2 inch frame keeps clearance for the roof edge. The listing cites a 30-year output warranty, which you should read for the actual degradation allowance.

Because the trailer's battery is usually at the tongue, wiring decides how much of that 400W you keep. Series wiring doubles the voltage and halves the current, so a thin run loses little, but it needs an MPPT controller with a suitable input window. The panels have no shade layout, so a roof air conditioner shadow across one panel hurts a series string.

Plan the layout so both panels sit forward of the air conditioner or well clear of it. Seal each foot, add a roof entry gland rather than a new hole, and check sealant yearly. Compared with the Callsun 100W pair, it has half the mounting points for the same total watts.
products.bestFor: Trailer owners who want 400W from only two panels and are ready for an MPPT controller.
pros: 400W from just two compact panels
N-type cells with up to 25.4% efficiency
46.3 by 30.1 inch size fits beside vents and the air conditioner
Fewer mounting points than a four-panel array
cons: No shade-tolerant layout, so an AC shadow hurts a series string
IP65 is a notch below IP68 panels

products.name: 400W Set, Two 200W N-Type Panels, -0.3%/C
products.description:
Heat is the quiet enemy of a roof panel on a trailer parked in a summer lot, and this set advertises a temperature coefficient of minus 0.3% per degree Celsius, better than older panels. That means for every degree above 25 C the panel loses about 0.3% of its power, so a 65 C roof costs roughly 12%. The cells are A+ grade N-type with up to 25.6% efficiency.

The listing also mentions built-in reverse blocking diodes that limit the damage from a passing shadow, though it does not publish the percentage of output retained. Treat it as a margin, not a guarantee. The set is configured for 12V or 24V banks, which gives flexibility if you later convert the trailer to a higher voltage.

The brand is unnamed in the listing, so verify warranty and support before buying. Mount with an air gap so heat can leave, and check the connectors each season. Compared with the HQST pair it leads on temperature behavior and is similar in watts.
products.bestFor: Trailers parked in hot, sunny climates where roof heat cuts output.
pros: Minus 0.3% per degree coefficient trims hot-roof losses
A+ N-type cells with up to 25.6% efficiency
Reverse blocking diodes help with shadows
Configurable for 12V or 24V banks
cons: Brand is unnamed, so warranty and support need checking
Shade benefit is not quantified in the listing

products.name: Callsun 200W Set, Two 100W N-Type Panels
products.description:
Two small 100W panels give a trailer 200W while leaving room around a crowded roof, and each module measures only 31.1 by 22.7 inches and weighs 11.4 lb. The N-type 16-busbar cells claim 25% efficiency with better light absorption and fewer hot spots than 9BB or 10BB designs. Wiring the pair in series or parallel is a free choice.

The small size is both strength and weakness. Each module needs its own feet and sealant, so four mounting points get you 200W where the HQST would take two for 400W. That is worth it if your roof is split by fixtures into narrow rectangles, and wasteful if you have open space.

The pair is a sensible entry level that can grow by adding another set. Keep the wiring short, fuse each string, and check sealant yearly. Next to the ECO-WORTHY 200W kit it gives better cells and a smaller footprint, but you supply the controller.
products.bestFor: Trailers with a roof broken into small gaps by vents and a skylight.
pros: 31.1 by 22.7 inch modules fit small roof gaps
N-type 16BB cells at up to 25% efficiency
Fewer hot spots than 9BB or 10BB designs
Easy to expand by adding another pair

products.name: ECO-WORTHY 200W Kit With 30A PWM Controller
products.description:
Everything for a basic trailer system arrives in one box: 200W of monocrystalline panels and a 30A PWM controller, with a claimed 800Wh a day in four hours of sun. The aluminum frame is corrosion resistant and rated for strong wind. It works with 12V or 24V banks.

The PWM controller is where the trailer's long cable run bites. A PWM controller wants the panel voltage near the battery voltage, so parallel wiring and thick cable are needed to the tongue, which adds cost the kit's cables rarely cover. An MPPT upgrade makes the long run much more efficient.

For a weekend trailer with a modest battery, the kit gets you working at a low price. Seal the feet, fuse near the battery and measure the run to the tongue before trusting the supplied wire. It is the cost-first choice, below the Callsun pair on cell quality.
products.bestFor: First-time trailer owners who want a complete and inexpensive 200W starter.
pros: Complete 200W kit with a 30A controller
Works with 12V or 24V battery banks
Corrosion-resistant aluminum frame
800Wh daily claim suits weekend use
cons: PWM controller loses efficiency on a long tongue cable run
Older monocrystalline cells give fewer watts per square foot

products.name: Renogy 100W Starter Kit With 30A PWM Controller
products.description:
One 100W panel and a 30A controller give a trailer the lightest possible entry into solar, with a claimed 500Wh a day. The listing cites UL 61730, CSA and IEC certification, and ratings of 2400Pa wind and 5400Pa snow. A ten-year coverage claim on panel materials adds some comfort.

At 100W it only keeps a modest battery topped up and runs lights and a fan, which is far less than the HQST pair can do. What the kit offers is a controller with plenty of headroom, so you can add panels later without a swap, though it remains PWM. For a trailer used for occasional weekends, it fits.

Mount it near the front of the roof to shorten the cable run to the tongue battery. Seal the feet and check the sealant each spring. It is the most affordable roof kit here and a good test of whether you want solar at all.
products.bestFor: Occasional weekend trailer owners adding solar for the first time.
pros: 30A controller leaves room to add panels later
UL 61730 and IEC 61215 certifications listed
Rated for 2400Pa wind and 5400Pa snow
Lowest-cost roof kit in the lineup
cons: 100W only keeps a small battery topped up
PWM controller wastes energy as the array grows

products.name: Go Power GP-PSK-130 Folding Kit With 10A Controller
products.description:
For a trailer parked in the shade, a folding kit that sets up in the sun makes sense, and Go Power supplies a 130W folding panel with a 10A controller and adjustable legs. It includes Anderson-style connectors, SAE and XLR plugs and ring terminals, so it can reach a battery or a trailer inlet.

The 130W output is modest, and a 10A controller caps the kit at about 140W at 12V, which is a good match for the panel but no room for growth. It will keep a trailer battery topped up on a long stay but will not run a fridge all day. The legs let you aim the panel without a prop.

Coil the cable loosely, and store the kit in its case. A portable kit has no roof penetrations, which suits renters and people who tow rarely. It complements a roof array on shady stays.
products.bestFor: Trailer owners who park in shade or want solar with no roof work.
pros: Folding panel moves out of the shade
Adjustable legs aim the panel without a prop
Many plug types for different inlets
No roof penetrations or sealant needed
cons: 10A controller leaves no room to expand

buyingCriteria.explanation: Most trailers carry batteries on the tongue, often 25 feet or more from the roof, so a long run of cable loses power as heat. Series wiring with an MPPT controller halves current and cuts those losses, which favors the HQST 400W pair. A thin cable on a PWM kit like the ECO-WORTHY can lose a noticeable share of its output.

A trailer parked in a sunny lot can see roof temperatures far above ambient, and panels lose power with heat. The 400W set rated at minus 0.3% per degree beats older panels that lose 0.4% or more. On a very hot day that difference adds up to double-digit percentages.

A trailer roof has an air conditioner, vents, a skylight and a satellite dish. Measure around them and keep panels out of the shadow of the air conditioner. A series string loses output sharply when one panel is shaded, so parallel wiring or a shade-tolerant panel helps.

Each panel needs feet, sealant and connectors, and each hole is a leak risk. Two 200W HQST panels give 400W with four mounting points, while four 100W panels need eight. Fewer, larger panels simplify the install if the roof has room.

MPPT controllers handle higher-voltage series strings and recover more energy than PWM, especially on a long cable run. The kits here use 30A PWM units, which suit 200W or less at 12V. For 400W, plan on a 30 to 40A MPPT controller.

A roof array charges all day with no effort, while a portable kit like the Go Power can move into the sun when the trailer sits in shade. A portable kit also avoids roof holes. Many owners combine a modest roof array with a portable panel.

howWeEvaluated.title: Roof footprint and count
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared module size and the mounting points needed for each watt. The HQST pair at 46.3 by 30.1 inches scored best for open roofs, and the Callsun 31.1 by 22.7 inch modules for tight ones. Fewer holes scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat and shade behavior
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for temperature coefficients and shade features. The 400W set's minus 0.3% per degree stood out, and the diodes gave a small credit. Single-string panels without features scored lowest.

howWeEvaluated.title: Long-run electrical fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed how each pick suits a long cable to a tongue battery. N-type panels with MPPT and series wiring scored high, and PWM kits scored lower. Missing voltage specs lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked controllers, plugs and brackets. The ECO-WORTHY and Renogy kits include controllers, the HQST and Callsun sets do not, and the Go Power kit includes plugs. We counted expansion headroom.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: Owner feedback patterns shaped our view of roof leaks, controller reliability and cable-run losses. We discounted warranty claims without terms.

howToChoose.subheading: PWM vs MPPT for a Trailer

cards.label: PWM
cards.text: The ECO-WORTHY and Renogy kits use PWM. It is simple and fine for 100 to 200W, but a long tongue cable run on 12V loses more.

cards.label: MPPT
cards.text: Series strings of the HQST or 400W set need MPPT. It cuts current, tolerates thin wire and recovers more energy in cold or hazy light.

howToChoose.note: Choose PWM for one or two small panels, MPPT as soon as you reach 400W.

rows: Short cable to a trailer inlet

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: 400W or more of panel, an MPPT controller, a lithium battery and a wiring plan for the tongue run. A fridge and electronics can use 1000Wh a day.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The HQST 400W pair with an MPPT controller fits the case, and the 400W N-type set adds hot-roof benefit.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You camp off-grid for days or park in hot sun. The HQST pair and the 400W set give you the output and heat behavior.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp in short trips with hookups. The Renogy 100W starter or the ECO-WORTHY 200W kit keep the battery topped up.

maintenance.why: Trailer roofs flex and bake, and sealant cracks. A leak at a panel foot can damage the roof deck.
A long cable to the tongue chafes at body seams. Look for worn insulation and warm connectors.
A trailer parked under trees collects debris. Use water and a soft cloth.

maintenance.task: Check battery state and controller settings
maintenance.why: Wrong settings or a loose terminal show up first as a battery that never fills.
Highway vibration loosens hardware. A loose panel can lift in the wind.

faq.q: How many panels does a travel trailer need?
faq.a: Two 200W panels cover most trailers for a fridge, lights and electronics. Add more if you boondock for days.

faq.q: Why is wiring to the tongue so important?
faq.a: A long run of thin cable loses power as heat. Series wiring with MPPT reduces current and loss.

faq.q: Can I run the trailer air conditioner on solar?
faq.a: Not with a typical roof array. It needs far more panel, battery and inverter capacity than 400W provides.
For light use, yes. A 130W portable kit keeps a battery topped up but will not run a fridge all day.
You can if you seal every hole. Prefer existing holes or a cable entry gland to limit leak points.

faq.q: What size controller do I need?
faq.a: Divide array watts by battery voltage and add headroom. A 400W array at 12V needs a controller above 30A, so choose 40A to be safe.
